drafts.title: Reliable voice control that correctly follows driving commands
drafts.description: When driving, the driver can speak common commands (navigation entry, phone calls, media, climate intents) and the car executes the intended action without re-speaking or long delays.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: In an in-vehicle noise test (simulated cabin noise at ~70 km/h), the system executes the intended action on first attempt in >=92% of 200 natural‑speech utterances and correctly handles >=95% of a validated set of 25 common driving commands (measured end‑to‑end, from utterance to action).
assumptions: Test uses a balanced dataset of accents and typical in-cabin noises (engine, road, wind, HVAC).
Microphones and audio processing are functioning per current BMW baseline.
OTA updates to improve models are possible during the model lifecycle.
uncertainties: Performance may vary with uncommon accents, heavy background music, or third‑party phone-based voice assistants.
Requirement assumes vendor cooperation for model updates and in-car microphone quality.

drafts.title: Reliable wireless phone charging that consistently charges placed phones
drafts.description: When a compatible phone is placed on the vehicle wireless pad using a normal user placement, it reliably starts and maintains charging through typical driving without frequent re-positioning or session dropouts.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: With three representative Qi‑compatible phones, placing the phone centrally on the pad begins charging within 5 seconds and increases battery level by >=10% within 30 minutes during mixed driving (city/highway); charging sessions experience no interruptions in >=95% of 200 real-world drive starts.
assumptions: Phones tested support widely used Qi profiles and are representative flagship and popular mid-range models at launch.
Users place phones roughly centered on the pad (normal use).
Testing includes typical vehicle vibrations and electromagnetic conditions.
uncertainties: Very thick cases, magnetic accessories or unsupported phone models may reduce performance.
Future phone designs could change alignment tolerances.

drafts.title: Clear, readable HUD and center screen in bright sunlight without manual adjustments
drafts.description: Critical HUD information (speed, active navigation prompt) and primary center-screen content (navigation text, key instrument readouts) remain legible in bright sunlight so drivers do not need to shade the display or manually change settings.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Under a controlled 10,000 lux sunlight simulation, 95% of test participants can (a) read HUD speed and next-turn instruction within 2 seconds and (b) read primary navigation text on the center screen within 2 seconds, without any manual brightness/contrast changes.
assumptions: 10,000 lux in-lab simulation approximates bright direct sunlight for typical daytime conditions.
Test participants have corrected-to-normal vision; common sunglasses may affect results.
Adaptive display software and hardware calibration at production are available.
uncertainties: Very dark polarized sunglasses or extreme viewing angles could reduce legibility for some users.
Different geographic daylight intensities and windshield coatings may change real-world results.

drafts.title: Tactile, glance-free climate controls for temperature and fan speed
drafts.description: Drivers can change cabin temperature and fan speed by touch alone, without looking away from the road, using clearly differentiated physical controls.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: In 100 blind-test trials (drivers keep eyes on the road), a driver can change cabin temperature by 2°C and change fan speed by one level by touch alone within 3 seconds in >=95% of trials.
assumptions: Controls are laid out with tactile differences (shape/texture) and provide clear haptic feedback when actuated.
Drivers are familiarized with control locations as part of normal delivery orientation.
uncertainties: Drivers with limited hand mobility or unusual glove use may have different success rates.
Exact control form factor (knob vs. buttons) will affect tactile discoverability.

drafts.title: Include heated steering wheel as standard in the Cold Weather package
drafts.description: Customers who select the Cold Weather package receive a heated steering wheel as a delivered feature without needing to add it separately as an expensive standalone option.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: 100% of vehicles configured and sold with the named 'Cold Weather' package include a heated steering wheel listed in the vehicle specification and delivered in the vehicle.
assumptions: Cold Weather package definition is standardized across markets for this vehicle generation.
Dealer ordering and VIN build processes will reflect the bundled content.
uncertainties: Regional variations in package names or regulatory limits could require mapping to an equivalent package.
Some legacy dealer ordering systems may need updates to prevent package splitting.

drafts.title: Customer requests for lower base price, cheaper lease, bundled/free packages, package discounts, lower dealer margin, subscriptions at requested price, or zero-percent financing (pricing and commercial requests)
drafts.description: Customers ask for lower MSRP below $50,000, lease rates cheaper than competitors, all option packages included in base, Comfort package 30% cheaper, lower dealer margins on options, heated-seats subscription at $15/month, and 0% financing offers.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Out of scope for product requirements: pricing, financing, dealer margin and subscription price levels are commercial decisions handled by pricing/finance teams and not specified as product engineering requirements here.
assumptions: These signals represent commercial and pricing preferences rather than product functional requirements.
uncertainties: Customer willingness-to-pay trade-offs and competitive pricing dynamics are outside the remit of this technical product backlog.
drafts.scope_reason: Pricing, financing, subscription fees and dealer margin decisions are commercial topics; out of scope for product technical requirements.

drafts.title: Requests for China CCC certification of infotainment (certification request)
drafts.description: Customers request that the infotainment system passes CCC certification for the Chinese market.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Out of scope for product requirements: regulatory/certification activities (CCC) are managed by compliance/regulatory teams and are not specified as product feature acceptance criteria here.
assumptions: Certification and homologation processes will be handled by the legal/compliance organization.
uncertainties: Specific technical changes required for certification are unknown until compliance teams engage with certifying authorities.
drafts.scope_reason: Regulation and homologation (CCC) are outside the product feature requirement scope; handled by compliance.

drafts.title: Requests that driver profile and data storage satisfy GDPR requirements (data protection / compliance request)
drafts.description: Customers ask that driver profiles and stored data satisfy GDPR requirements for data handling and deletion.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Out of scope for product requirements: legal and certification compliance tasks (GDPR) are managed by legal/privacy teams and are not defined as product feature acceptance criteria here.
assumptions: Privacy controls and compliance processes will be specified and validated by the privacy/legal organization.
Product teams will implement privacy controls per legal guidance but the legal acceptability is judged by the privacy team.
uncertainties: Interpretation of specific GDPR requirements for features (data retention windows, export/delete flows) may evolve with regulation guidance.
drafts.scope_reason: Regulatory and legal compliance (GDPR) are out of scope for product technical requirements; handled by legal/privacy.

drafts.title: Request to use a specific cockpit chip (Snapdragon 8295) — engineering spec request
drafts.description: Customers ask that the cockpit computer uses the Snapdragon 8295 chip.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Out of scope: requests for a named chip are an engineering/part-level specification and not a customer-facing product requirement; hardware component selection is handled in engineering BOM and platform decisions.
assumptions: Customers express desire for perceived performance improvements but do not specify a customer-level outcome beyond performance.
Actual hardware selection will be made by engineering considering lifecycle, supply and cost.
uncertainties: Component availability, lifecycle and supplier constraints may prevent use of a specific chip at production.
Customer-perceived improvements should be translated into performance targets rather than a specific part.
drafts.scope_reason: Specific component/part requests are engineering specifications and out of scope for customer-facing product requirements.
